conceptTag: Should a brand sell a division?
readerTitle: Is your company still the best owner of that division?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 제조사의 운송 부문, 근무 일정 소프트웨어의 급여 부가 기능) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업부를 팔지 말지는 수익성이 아니라 '우리가 이 사업의 가장 좋은 주인인가'로 판단하고, 분리한 뒤에도 남겨야 할 진짜 연결은 계약이나 제휴로 지킨다.
misconception: 돈을 버는 사업부는 계속 가지고 있어야 하고, 핵심이 아닌 사업부는 무조건 빨리 파는 게 맞다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: 포트폴리오 사고(STR-09-06), 스핀오프(STR-09-05)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 회사와 수치(트럭 30대, 물량 60%, 엔지니어 4분의 1 등)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 기업 사실이나 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.
'스핀오프'는 엄밀히는 주주에게 새 회사 지분을 나눠 주는 방식입니다. 가족 기업 사례이므로 카드에서는 '매각 또는 별도 회사로 분리'로 넓게 쓰고, 특정 국가의 법률·세무 절차는 다루지 않았습니다. STR-09-05 정의와 표현이 맞는지 확인하세요.
'dis-synergies'(분리 후 공유 비용이 두 배가 되는 현상) 용어가 STR-09-02/05에서 쓰는 표현과 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The trucks that outgrew the pans
body: A family cookware brand makes pans in one factory. Twenty years ago it bought a few trucks to deliver its own goods. Today the trucking arm runs 30 trucks, and other companies fill a growing share of its loads.
It makes money. Yet every budget meeting ends the same way: the factory gets the new machine, and the trucks wait.

image.label: A cookware factory with a small truck fleet parked beside it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 프라이팬 공장, 오른쪽에 트럭 여러 대가 줄지어 서 있음. 공장 쪽에는 새 기계가 들어오고 트럭 쪽은 그늘져 기다리는 분위기. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A logistics firm wants to buy your trucks.
body: Before you even look at the price, which question matters most?

options.feedback: Useful, but a profitable unit can still be held back by its owner. Profit tells you it's a good business, not that you're the right home for it.

options.text: Are we the best owner for it, or could someone else make it worth more?
options.feedback: This is portfolio thinking: judge each unit by what you add to it and what it adds to you, not by its profit alone.

options.text: Is it part of our core? If not, sell.
options.feedback: Fast and tidy, but it skips how much the brand still depends on those trucks. Selling on a label can cut a link you need.

cards.title: A good business with the wrong parent.
body: The fleet manager wants ten new trucks to win a regional contract. The board keeps choosing a new pan line instead, because pans are what the family knows.
Some of the fleet's customers are other kitchen brands. They hesitate to share shipping volumes with a rival's subsidiary.
And the brand gets nothing special from owning trucks. A good outside carrier could ship its pans at a similar cost.

cards.title: Who adds the most value to this unit?
body: **Portfolio thinking** asks what role each unit plays and whether you are its **best owner**: the one who can make it worth the most.

Here the answer is uncomfortable. The brand starves the trucks of capital, scares off some of their customers, and gains no edge in return. A logistics company would fund them, focus on them and sell their capacity freely.

image.label: Two owners compared: what each adds to the truck fleet
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 가운데 트럭 아이콘. 왼쪽 'Cookware brand' 쪽 화살표에는 "Little capital", "Rival brands hesitate", 오른쪽 'Logistics firm' 쪽 화살표에는 "Funding", "Focus", "Open to all shippers". 오른쪽이 더 굵은 화살표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: But you still need those trucks.
body: About 60% of the fleet's loads are still your pans, and peak-season deliveries to big retailers depend on it. How do you separate?

options.text: Sell to the logistics firm, no strings attached
options.feedback: You get the cleanest deal, but your peak season now rests on a carrier with no promise to you. You'd trade a capital problem for a delivery risk.

options.text: Sell or set it up as a separate company, with a multi-year shipping contract at market rates
options.feedback: This is spin-off logic: separation gives each business its own focus and funding, while a contract keeps the one link that's real.

options.text: Keep it, but give it its own budget and board
options.feedback: It eases the capital fight, but rival brands still see a competitor's trucks. You fix part of the problem and keep the owner who caused it.

cards.title: Separating costs more than it looks.
body: Shared things must be split: accounting, IT, the depot, even some managers. Costs that were shared now get paid twice. These **dis-synergies** can eat much of the gain.
The contract needs care too. Too long, and you're locked into an old price. Too short, and you're exposed in peak season.
And selling in a hurry to the first bidder usually leaves money on the table. The test: does a better owner create more value than the cost of untangling?

image.label: Shared services being split in two
image.brief: 하나의 사무실 건물이 두 개로 갈라지는 일러스트. 갈라진 틈에 'Accounting', 'IT', 'Depot' 상자가 두 개씩 복제되어 있음. 비용이 늘어난다는 느낌을 동전 더미로 표현. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your app schedules shifts for restaurants and shops. Five years ago you built a small payroll add-on. Payroll rules differ by country, so a quarter of your engineers now just keep it legal.
Users who use both products churn less. A payroll specialist offers to buy the add-on. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it. Lower churn is worth the engineers
options.feedback: The retention is real, but ask where it comes from: owning payroll, or the connection between the two? If it's the connection, you're paying a quarter of your team for something a partner could provide.

options.text: Sell it to the specialist, with a deep integration and joint offer
options.feedback: Portfolio thinking says the specialist is the better owner. Spin-off logic says keep the real link, here through integration, so users keep the combined experience.

options.text: Shut it down and move the engineers to scheduling
options.feedback: You free the team fast, but customers suddenly lose payroll and may leave with it. You give up both the sale price and the retention.

cards.title: Ask who should own it, then how to stay connected.
body: This lesson used two ideas from this unit:
list: **Portfolio thinking:** judge a division by whether you are its best owner, not just by its profit.
**Spin-offs:** separation can free a unit to grow, as long as you protect the links that are real and count the cost of untangling.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick one product line or team. Write down what you give it that no one else could, and what it gives you. If both lists are short, it may belong elsewhere.
